narrative:
The model predicted a 75% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the admissions process uses this prediction to assess risk, your application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by your academic performance during law school. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest factor pushing the model toward predicting failure; you placed in the second decile, noticeably lower than the average of roughly sixth-decile among students who were accepted. Your first-year ranking was the second most important factor and also pulled the prediction toward failure, as you again ranked in the second decile compared with an average of sixth-decile for accepted students. These two early indicators of how you performed relative to your classmates outweighed everything else.

Your LSAT score was the only major factor that worked in your favor. At 38 it sat slightly above the average of accepted students, giving the model some reason to expect you might pass. Unfortunately, this positive signal was not strong enough to overcome the clear pattern shown by your law-school grades.

You should focus on strengthening your academic record if you retake courses or enroll in a post-graduation bar-preparation program that emphasizes consistent high performance. Improving your class standing in future work will directly address the factors that most hurt your prediction.
